THREE VIEWS SHOWING NATIONAL ARMY MEN IN CHARGE "OVER THE TOP" AND INTO THE EMY PRINCHEES.

Three most unusual photos showing National Army men going over the top and into the enemy trenches. The top photo shows the men running up the incline with their bayonets fixed starting for the enemy trenches. The centre photo shows the men reaching the edge of the incline, and several of them have already jumped into the enemy "trench" and got their man. The lower photo shows Uncle San's fighters down in the enemy trenches jabbing the "enemy" with their bayonets. The enemy in this case is a bundle of branches.

The photographs show graphically how strenuous and real the training of the National Army men in the various cantonments is. The training is not ploy. It is real as it can be made under the circumstances. GINSORD AND RASSED BY THE COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC INFORMATION.

PEOPLE WE READ ABOUT.

Four young Southernors, three of them sons of cx-Governors and the other son of a Governor, in the Officers Training Camp at Fort MacPherson, Georgia. They are, from left to right: Charles Brown, son of ex-Governor Brown of Georgia; Hugh Comer; son of ex-Governor Comer of Alabama; S.J. Catts, Jr., son of Governor Catts of Florida; and Dan Fowle, son of ex-Governor Fowle of North Carolina.

Governors' sons are numerous at this training camp for the Officers' Reserve Corps. It is located at Fort MacPherson, Georgia. The young-men of the South are in no way behind their Northern or Western cousins. They have flocked to the training camp and are taking the work quite as seriously and just as enthusiastically as the men now at the original Plattsburg camp in New York.

BARBED WIRE FENCE CHARGED WITH HIGH CURRENT SURROUNDS COUNTRY'S LARGEST RADIO PLANT.
Seven foot barbed wire fence which surrounds country's largest radio plant at Callos Heights near San Diego, Calif.
Photo also shows U. S. soldier on guard, one of the detachment that patrols the grounds of the station day and night.
The plant is the largest atation in the United States. The towers are over 600 feet in height. Messages from this plant have been sent to Berlin and received from that city.

Washington recently ordered that the station be carefully guarded and a barbed wire fence seven feet high was erected around the grounds. The wire is charged with 30,600 volts. In addition to this effective barrier the plant is guarded day and night by U.S. soldiers. No one is permitted entrance to the station or surrounding territory unless properly identified and vouched for.

For these young men in civil life, who have no trade or profession, an opportunity is offered in the U.S. Army. During an enlistment of one or two years, a man is given an opportunity to learn a trade or profession to prepay himself for the outside business world. And special efforts are made to develop self reliance, initiative perseverance and judgement. He must not pay any tuition, but is paid $30, or more a month, while learning. These young men are learning printing and type compositing and come in contact with obstacles exactly the same as they would meet in every day civil life.

EVENTS WE READ ABOUT.
FUTURE ARMY OFFICERS RECEIVE INSTRUCTION, THEORETICAL AND PRACTICAL.

The "Plattsburg" camps throughout the United States are just about getting into the swing. Companies have been formed, duties assigned, programs arranged, and things are beginning to settle down and take shape.

There is no consistency at any of the training camps. The men go there to be instructed in the duties and requirements of an officer. They learn military technique, familiarize themselves with ordinance, and receive lectures; their instruction is both theoretical and practical.

During certain periods of the day the men form in some spot near the camp and sitting in a circle or convenient position listen to a dissertation on some time-ly subject delivered by an experienced army officer. These little impromptu talks go far toward interesting the men and reusing enthusiasm, and besides the men acquire knowledge they could not learn from any text book.
Photograph shows company of future army officers seated in a circle listening to an explanation of "why's and wherefore's" by an army officer. 5/19/17.

"GET THEM BOYS," BAYONET CHARGE BY UNCLE SAM'S COMING OFFDERS.

Over a rail fence in a fierce bayonet charge in one of the Officers' Reserve Corps "some" where in the United States." The training of Uncle Sam's coming officers is a rigorous test for the young men. To be able to go thru the strenuous drilling, the men must be physically perfect. The bayonet charging is an important part of their training. The old U.Sstyle of bayonet charging has been completely revised, and it now resembles the English style a great deal. The new method puts more power in the thrust and also lessens the chance of being stopped by the fee. The photo shows the men in the air as they leaped over a roughly-constructed hurdle or rail fence.

FRECH AIR HEROES ARRIVE HERE TO INSTRUCT AMERICAN FLIERS.

French aviators who have just arrived in America to advise and instruct American fliers. The photo was taken in front of the Aero Club of America in New York City, just before the officers left for an inspection tour of a nearby aviator's training camp! Standing to the extreme left, in civilian dress, is Allan R. Hawley, president of the Aero Club of America. To the right, in civilian dress, is Rear, ADMIRAL BRADLEY A. Fiske, U.S.H., retired.

The party is composed of picked French officers every one of whom has been cited and decorated. They have come from the Champagne front, and were given just four days notice to proceed to the U.S. Capt. Boyrinen commands the party. Three of his mutants have the Legion of Honor. One of his men who has flown on every front has over ten decorations.

In the captain's opinion the French and English now have a clear superiority of the air, surpassing the Germans in morale and machines. He says the U.S. can do no greater service than the concentrate its energies on an air fleet.
The officers will proceed soon to Washington and will then be assigned to various aviation training stations to instruct American aviators in flying.

Cadets at the United States Military Academy, West Point are getting more severe training than usual. Their training has been speeded up so that the next graduation class can get in the field about August, months before their normal time.

COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY BATTALION GETS REAL WAR TRAULING,

The Columbia UniversityKKUttalion is in camp "some where in the United States" and they're getting sealed war practices. Their curriculum covers every branch of the fighting service, offensive and defensive. Marching, trinesh construction, building of engineering projects, target practice, bomb-throwing, and field tactics and manoeuvres all take place on the camp's program. "Lt. Hodder Williams of Princess's Registry, Canada, who was wounded at the Bonnig is directing field operations. The students are getting practical knowledge of military operations. Many of them are qualifying for entrance into the Blattsburg camps, seeking to obtain commissions in the United States Reserve.

The old adage "music hath charms to soothe the soul." does not exclude Uncle Sam's husky Marines, and they are giver a thirty minute lesson in vocalizing by a regular musical instructor every other day. Singing is considered a necessity and the boys are encouraged to sing as much as possible. What is there more relieving than to hear a tuneful melody after a long march, or after strenuous drilling or fighting? The boys are being taught popular songs and a lot of the old favorites so whenever they feel like a song they can all burst out with a song and have real harmony. The class is large and when the sea soldiers sing they make quite a bit of noise. The voices are good, and it is a pleasure to hear this "Glee Club." JABBING THE KAHER.-GREATEST OF OUT DOOR SPORTS AT NATIONAL ARMY CAMPS.

The favorite out door sport of the boys who are learning to be soldiers at the National Army camps all over the United States is jabbing Kaiser Bill. Of course the fact that the only Kaiser they can jab is a dummy takes some of the joy out of the pastime, but at that the soldier in the photo is enjoying himself.

This dummy Kaiser was set up for bayonet practice at Camp Dix. His heart is marked out plainly so that the boys who go through this training will know just where to plunge their bayonets when they meet the Kaiser's men, they hope to meet him too, somewhere along the Western front. This jabbing the Kaiser is good fun but at the same time it is mighty good practice in the science of manipulating the bayonet which is a very important item in the education of every good fighting man.
